modalities.name: Clean Slate Pickup
modalities.tagline: A captainless game where every point starts from zero.
modalities.whatItIs: Clean Slate Pickup is a drop-in team game, such as Ultimate, in which nothing from the past is allowed to count. Teams are redrawn before every point, no score is carried over and nobody becomes known as the best or worst player. It pushes team sport even further from imagery and personal history, the ground of Ideal Parent Figure work, toward pure, player-run present tense.
modalities.coreIdea: When teams, scores and reputations reset every point, all that is left is the play happening right now, run entirely by the players.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twelve to twenty players meet at a park for about 90 minutes, warm up together, then draw colored bibs from a bag before each point to form new teams. Each point is played flat out and then let go: no tally, no stats, no captains and no coach, and calls are settled by the two players involved. The session ends with a short circle where people name one moment they enjoyed, not who won.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel boxed in by labels, rankings or their own history, and anyone who wants a fast, sociable game with no pecking order.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed sprinting and cutting bring leg injuries and a risk of head knocks, so warm up, build fitness gradually, stop playing after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea and is not a substitute for therapy for attachment or relationship difficulties.
modalities.tweet: Fresh concept: Clean Slate Pickup. A drop-in game where teams are redrawn every point, nobody keeps score and no one has a reputation, so every point starts from zero. For anyone tired of labels and rankings who just wants to play hard, right now.

modalities.name: One Body Drills
modalities.tagline: Structured drills where the whole team moves as one.
modalities.whatItIs: One Body Drills is a training format in which the unit of play is the whole team, not the individual player. Every drill asks all seven players to move together, so attention goes fully to teammates rather than to inner voices. It pushes team sport away from inward parts work such as Internal Family Systems, toward outward coordination, with a little more structure than a normal practice.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving as one coordinated body with others can make belonging something you feel in your legs and eyes, not just an idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 75-minute session, a team works through set drills: a zone defense that shifts together on one call, a passing chain in which every player must touch the disc before a score counts, and mirrored cuts done in pairs and then in sevens. A volunteer runs the drills from a printed card, and each drill ends only when the whole group, not the fastest player, completes it cleanly. The session closes with a game in which a point counts only if everyone touched the disc.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy teamwork more than personal glory, and anyone who wants to feel part of something moving together.
modalities.cautions: Repeated sprints and sudden changes of direction can strain knees and ankles, so warm up well, rest between drills, drink water and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. This is an untested concept, and sport supports but does not replace mental health care.
modalities.tweet: What if a team practice saw the whole team as one body? One Body Drills: zone shifts on one call, passing chains where everyone must touch the disc, all seven moving together. An untested idea for people who love teamwork more than solo glory.

modalities.name: Rule Jam Games
modalities.tagline: A team game whose rules are invented and dropped as you play.
modalities.whatItIs: Rule Jam Games is loose, playful team sport with no fixed rulebook, no score kept past each round and no plan to improve. Players start from a simple disc or ball game and invent, change or drop rules on the spot. It sits beyond team sport, away from structured, goal-driven talking therapy such as CBT: less agenda, less correcting, more letting the game become whatever the group makes of it.
modalities.coreIdea: Play without a plan: the game grows out of what the group does in the moment, and nothing needs to be corrected or measured.
modalities.whatYouDo: A mixed group meets on a field for an hour with a few discs, balls and cones. Every ten minutes anyone can propose a new rule, such as 'throws must be backhand' or 'two discs at once', and a quick show of hands keeps it or drops it. Nobody keeps score beyond the current round, and the hour ends early if the group runs out of energy or ideas.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sport too rigid, competitive or rule-bound, and anyone who misses unplanned play.
modalities.cautions: Improvised rules can lead to collisions or awkward movements, so agree on two safety rules that never change (no contact, no diving) and warm up first; anyone with heart or joint problems should check with a doctor first. It is an untested idea, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: An idea for grown-ups who miss real play: Rule Jam Games. Start with a disc, invent a rule, vote it in or out every ten minutes and never keep score past the round. No plan, no stats, just a game that becomes whatever the group makes of it.

modalities.name: Silent Signal Matches
modalities.tagline: Full-speed team games played without a single spoken word.
modalities.whatItIs: Silent Signal Matches are ordinary team games, such as Ultimate, played under one extra rule: nobody speaks. Teammates coordinate through eye contact, pointing, timing and a handful of agreed hand signals, and even disputed calls are settled with signs. It moves team sport away from word-based therapy such as ACT, with its talk of values and thoughts, toward pure body-to-body communication.
modalities.coreIdea: Taking words out of the game means teamwork has to happen through the eyes and body, so people connect and cooperate without explaining themselves.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 90-minute session, the group spends ten minutes learning six hand signals, for example for 'I'm open', 'foul' and 'replay the point'. Games are then played at full speed in total silence, with a short spoken break at halftime to adjust the signals. The session ends with players sharing, out loud this time, what they noticed about teammates when nobody could talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find talking draining or feel they always over-explain, and teams that want sharper teamwork without words.
modalities.cautions: Without shouted warnings collisions are more likely, so play no-contact, keep a whistle or a loud clap for emergencies and warm up properly; check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested concept, and some people find enforced silence uncomfortable, so it should stay optional.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Silent Signal Matches. A full-speed team game where nobody says a word. You read eyes, point, time your cuts and settle calls with hand signs. For anyone tired of talking who wants to connect with people through movement instead. 🤫

modalities.name: Snap Decision Disc
modalities.tagline: A game too fast to think: throw within three seconds.
modalities.whatItIs: Snap Decision Disc is a fast version of a throwing team game in which the disc must leave your hand within a count of three, instead of the usual ten in Ultimate. Every throw becomes a split-second choice, so there is no time to weigh options or second-guess. It sits beyond team sport, away from slow, meaning-seeking work such as Coherence Therapy, which looks for what lies under a reaction; here the reaction is the whole point.
modalities.coreIdea: When the game moves faster than deliberation, people get to practice acting on instinct and letting a mistake go the moment it happens.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of five play 15-minute games on a short field, with the marker counting 'one, two, three' aloud on every catch. A dropped or rushed throw is simply a turnover, and the one rule of the session is that nobody comments on mistakes. Sessions last about an hour, including a warm-up of quick-release passing in pairs.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who overthink, replay their choices or freeze when there is no perfect option, and anyone who enjoys fast, chaotic play.
modalities.cautions: Rushed throws and fast cuts raise the risk of collisions, finger knocks and leg strains, so warm up, play no-contact, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea and is no replacement for help with anxiety or perfectionism.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Snap Decision Disc. You must throw within three seconds, so there is no time to weigh options or second-guess yourself, and nobody comments on mistakes. For overthinkers who want an hour of pure instinct with other people.

modalities.name: Big Field Festival
modalities.tagline: A monthly mass game for dozens of players at once.
modalities.whatItIs: Big Field Festival is team sport at crowd scale: 30 to 60 people, several fields, teams reshuffled every half hour and a lot of shouting, calling and laughing. It pushes team sport as far as it goes from solitary, quiet, body-calming work such as TRE shaking, toward maximum social contact and energy. The body is busy, but so is the talk, from introductions to calls to strategy between games.
modalities.coreIdea: Social energy grows with numbers, so a game big enough to meet dozens of people in one afternoon makes belonging feel large and loud.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a month, volunteers mark out three or four small fields in a park for a three-hour drop-in. Players are sorted into new mixed teams every 30 minutes, so each person plays with and against dozens of others, and everyone swaps names in a quick huddle before each game. Between rounds there is water, shade and a shared snack table, and the afternoon ends with one giant circle.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are new to a city, want a lot of social contact quickly or feel lifted by crowds and noise.
modalities.cautions: Three hours of play brings fatigue, heat and injury risk, so sit out rounds freely, drink often, play no-contact, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested concept, and big crowds can feel overwhelming for some people, so a quiet space on the sideline helps.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: Big Field Festival 🥏 A monthly drop-in game for 30 to 60 people, new mixed teams every half hour and names swapped before every game. An untested idea for anyone new in town who wants to meet a crowd by playing with them.

modalities.name: Skill Ladder Sessions
modalities.tagline: One team skill per week, climbed rung by rung.
modalities.whatItIs: Skill Ladder Sessions turn team practice into a step-by-step climb: each week the group picks one skill, such as a forehand throw or a defensive mark, and works up a ladder of drills that get harder. It moves team sport away from slow, wait-and-listen inner practices such as Focusing, toward active, deliberate improvement. Players run it themselves, with a printed ladder instead of a coach.
modalities.coreIdea: Progress is made, not waited for: small, visible steps up a skill ladder give everyone a concrete sense of getting better together.
modalities.whatYouDo: A 90-minute session starts with a warm-up, then players move through five drill stations for the week's skill, each harder than the last, stepping up a rung once they pass a simple test such as eight good throws out of ten. Partners give each other one tip per round. The final half hour is a game in which using the week's skill earns a bonus point.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like clear progress and feedback, and teammates of mixed ability who want a structured way to improve together.
modalities.cautions: Repetitive throwing and fast drills can strain shoulders, knees and ankles, so warm up, vary the drills, rest and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and tests can make some players anxious, so the ladder should stay friendly and optional.
modalities.tweet: A new kind of team practice: Skill Ladder Sessions. Pick one skill a week, climb five drills that get harder, move up a rung when you pass, then play a game that rewards it. Made for people who love seeing themselves get better with friends.

modalities.name: Bracket Day Challenge
modalities.tagline: A player-run, one-day friendly tournament with brackets.
modalities.whatItIs: Bracket Day Challenge is a self-organized, one-day tournament in which teams play short games through a bracket toward a small, silly trophy. It moves team sport away from slow, presence-based coaching such as Aletheia, which avoids self-improvement, toward structure, goals and rising to a challenge. Everything, from the schedule to the calls, is run by the players.
modalities.coreIdea: A friendly, structured challenge with a clear goal lets a team rise to pressure together and then let it go at the end of the day.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to eight teams of mixed ability sign up, and a volunteer posts the bracket in the morning. Games last 20 minutes with 10-minute breaks, so each team plays four or five times by mid-afternoon, and every team, winners or not, ends in the final circle. Teams take turns with jobs such as scorekeeping, water and timing.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy friendly competition and goals, and teams that want a day to aim for together.
modalities.cautions: Several games in one day bring fatigue, heat and a higher risk of strains and collisions, so rest between games, drink water, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Competition can add stress rather than ease it, so keep the stakes low; this is an untested idea, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Bracket Day Challenge. A one-day, player-run tournament with short games, a bracket and a ridiculous trophy, for teams who want a shared goal and a little friendly pressure, then a big circle where everyone celebrates. 🏆

modalities.name: Called Play Practice
modalities.tagline: A playbook of set plays, each run on a single call.
modalities.whatItIs: Called Play Practice is team training built around a small playbook: a few set plays, each started by a one-word call and rehearsed until every player knows exactly where to run. It sits beyond team sport, as far as possible from Do Nothing meditation, in which nothing is steered. Here everything is deliberate: timing, spacing and intention, coordinated across a whole team.
modalities.coreIdea: Practicing deliberate, shared control, where everyone knows the plan and moves on cue, can give people a strong sense of competence and coordination.
modalities.whatYouDo: A player-coach leads a 90-minute session in which the team learns two or three set plays from a whiteboard, walks them, jogs them and then runs them at full speed on the call. Each play is repeated until it works three times in a row, and the last half hour is a game in which every set play is used at least twice. Players keep a small playbook card to study between sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like plans, precision and knowing their role, and anyone who finds unstructured play stressful.
modalities.cautions: Repeating full-speed sprints can cause muscle strains and fatigue, so warm up, build intensity gradually, rest between repetitions and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested concept, and a strong focus on perfect execution can turn into pressure, so mistakes should be part of the plan.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Called Play Practice. Your team learns three set plays, each started by one word, and drills them until everyone moves on cue. For people who love a plan, a clear role and the feeling of a whole team moving exactly as designed.

modalities.name: Three Disc Mayhem
modalities.tagline: A team game with three discs in play at once.
modalities.whatItIs: Three Disc Mayhem is a loose, chaotic team game played with three discs live at the same time, so there is always more happening than one person can track. It moves team sport away from metta and jhana meditation, where attention settles deeply on one warm inner feeling, toward wide, outward, constantly shifting attention. Rules are minimal and the mood is playful.
modalities.coreIdea: When too much is happening to lock onto any one thing, attention has to stay wide, open and pointed outward, toward the field and the people on it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play 10-minute rounds on a normal field, and each team can score with any of the three discs, while a score with one disc does not stop the others. Players call out names constantly so that passes can find them, and nobody tracks the total score. A session lasts about an hour, with short breaks between rounds.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get stuck in their heads, find stillness hard or simply love noisy, unpredictable games.
modalities.cautions: With several discs flying, the risk of being hit or colliding goes up, so use soft discs, play no-contact, keep your eyes up, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the chaos may feel overwhelming to some players.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if a team game had three discs in play at once? Three Disc Mayhem keeps your attention wide, outward and moving, with no time to sink into your own head. For people who love noisy, unpredictable games with friends.

modalities.name: Celebrate Every Catch
modalities.tagline: Team games where every good moment gets a loud celebration.
modalities.whatItIs: Celebrate Every Catch is a recreational team game with one cultural rule: every good catch, throw, block or effort gets a visible, shared celebration. It moves team sport away from vipassana, which trains watching experience without reacting, toward reacting on purpose, together and out loud. The sideline is part of the game, cheering what it sees and inventing small rituals.
modalities.coreIdea: Deliberately amplifying shared reactions, with cheers, high fives and naming each other's good moments, turns small wins into moments the whole team feels together.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a weekly 90-minute game, each team agrees on two or three celebrations, such as a group shout or a sideline tunnel, and uses them for every score and every great effort, the opponents' included. Players on the sideline call out specific things they saw, such as 'great cut!' or 'what a block!'. The game ends with each player naming one teammate's best moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rarely hear praise or find it hard to celebrate themselves, and anyone who loves an enthusiastic team atmosphere.
modalities.cautions: High energy can push players past their limits, so keep warm-ups, water breaks and a no-contact rule, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and constant attention can feel uncomfortable for shy players, so celebrations should be invitations, not demands.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Celebrate Every Catch. A team game where every good throw, catch or effort gets a shared celebration, opponents included, and the sideline cheers what it sees. For anyone who rarely hears 'nice one!' and could use a weekly dose of it. 🙌

modalities.name: Everyone Plays League
modalities.tagline: A slower, mixed-ability game built so anyone can join in.
modalities.whatItIs: Everyone Plays League is a gentler form of team sport, with no sprinting, generous substitutions and teams that mix ages and fitness levels. It moves team sport away from high-intensity interval training, toward lower effort, looser structure and more room for whatever the day brings. The social side leads: games pause for a laugh, a chat or a new player joining.
modalities.coreIdea: Lowering the intensity removes the fitness barrier, so the belonging and fun of a team can reach people who would never join a competitive side.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week, mixed teams of eight to ten play 15-minute games at a jog or brisk walk, with a no-sprinting rule and rolling substitutions so nobody sits out for long. Newcomers are paired with a buddy for their first game. Every session ends with tea or a snack together, and there is no league table.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel too old, unfit or out of practice for sport, families who want to play together, and anyone easing back in after illness or injury with their doctor's approval.
modalities.cautions: Even gentle play involves turns and the odd quick movement, so warm up, keep a no-contact rule and check with a doctor first if you have heart, joint or other health problems. It is an untested concept and supports, but does not replace, any care someone already has.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who think team sport isn't for them: Everyone Plays League. No sprinting, mixed ages and fitness levels, rolling subs, a buddy for newcomers and tea afterwards. Belonging first, fitness second.

modalities.name: Five Game Rotation
modalities.tagline: Five short, different team games in one evening.
modalities.whatItIs: Five Game Rotation is team sport built on variety: one evening, five quick team games and new teams for each. It pushes team sport away from steady, solo endurance exercise, which keeps one even rhythm for a long time, toward constant switching, stop-start effort and lots of different people. The rotation is set in advance, so the structure is clear even when the games are chaotic.
modalities.coreIdea: Changing game, rhythm and teammates every ten minutes keeps attention fresh and gives many more chances to connect than one long game.
modalities.whatYouDo: A group of 15 to 30 meets for 75 minutes and rotates through five 10-minute games, for example a disc game, a ball game, a relay, a tag game and a team target game, with a minute to reshuffle teams in between. A volunteer runs the timer and posts the rotation. The evening ends with everyone voting on which game stays in next week's rotation.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get bored easily, dislike long steady exercise or want to meet many people quickly.
modalities.cautions: Switching games means many quick starts and turns, so warm up well, play no-contact, pace yourself and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested concept, not a replacement for any care you already have.
modalities.tweet: New format idea: Five Game Rotation. One evening, five 10-minute team games, new teams for every one, then everyone votes which game survives to next week. Made for people who get bored with one long workout and want to meet lots of people.

modalities.name: Chase and Dodge Club
modalities.tagline: Adult chase games where speed and lightness beat strength.
modalities.whatItIs: Chase and Dodge Club is a loose, playful team activity made of chase games such as tag, capture the flag and keep-away, played by adults for fun. It moves team sport away from strength training, with its loads, counts and steady progress, toward lightness, evasion and play that is not trying to build anything. Nobody counts reps, keeps stats or follows a plan.
modalities.coreIdea: Light, quick, evasive play, with nothing to measure or improve, lets people experience their bodies as fast and free rather than as projects.
modalities.whatYouDo: About twenty adults meet in a park for an hour and play a string of chase games, each chosen by whoever suggests the next one. Teams form and dissolve quickly, rules stay simple, and there is a lot of laughing and running in short bursts. Anyone can step out at any time and rejoin when ready.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who dislike gyms and numbers, feel their exercise has become a chore, or want to play rather than train.
modalities.cautions: Sudden sprints, dodges and tags can cause falls, strains and collisions, so pick soft, even ground, use light two-finger tags, warm up and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: What if adult exercise looked like recess? Chase and Dodge Club: an hour of tag, capture the flag and keep-away, with no reps, no stats and no plan. An untested idea for anyone whose workouts feel like homework and who wants to feel fast and light.

modalities.name: Self-Run Showdown
modalities.tagline: Competitive games run entirely by the players, with no officials.
modalities.whatItIs: Self-Run Showdown is a competitive league with no referees, coaches or organizers: players make every call, set the schedule, pick the teams and review their own rules. It pushes team sport away from animal-assisted therapy, with its calm, professional-led sessions, toward full peer self-governance at full intensity. It takes the self-refereeing spirit of Ultimate as far as it can go.
modalities.coreIdea: Running everything yourselves, including settling disputes face to face, turns honesty, fairness and calm disagreement into skills practiced at full speed.
modalities.whatYouDo: A weekly league of four to six teams plays 60-minute games, and any disputed call is settled by the players involved within one minute, or the point is replayed. Each month every team sends one player to a short meeting that reviews the rules and how disputes went. There is no paid staff, and scheduling, fields and equipment rotate among members.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want intense competition with more trust and responsibility, and anyone who wants practice in standing their ground and calmly backing down.
modalities.cautions: Hard competitive play brings injury risk, especially to knees, ankles and heads, so warm up, keep it no-contact, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Disputes can get heated, so agree a cooling-off rule in advance; this is an untested idea, not therapy.
modalities.tweet: Invented practice: Self-Run Showdown. A competitive league with no refs, coaches or organizers. Players make every call, settle disputes face to face in under a minute and run it all together. For people who want intensity plus trust and responsibility.

modalities.name: Tiny Field Blitz
modalities.tagline: Three against three on a tiny field, all bursts.
modalities.whatItIs: Tiny Field Blitz shrinks a team game to three players a side on a field a quarter of the normal size, in short, intense games. It pushes team sport away from slow, calm, breath-led practices such as qigong, toward maximum activation, constant sprinting and nonstop involvement. There are almost no set plays, just reacting to the next pass.
modalities.coreIdea: Shrinking the field puts everyone in every moment, so intensity, attention and connection with teammates peak together.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a thorough warm-up, groups of six to twelve play 4-minute games of three against three with 2-minute rests, for about 45 minutes. Every player touches the disc or ball several times a minute, and teams rotate after each game. A cool-down walk and stretch end the session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Fit people short on time who love intensity, and anyone who drifts off during big, slow games.
modalities.cautions: Near-maximal effort and constant changes of direction put real strain on the heart, knees and ankles, so build fitness first, warm up thoroughly, rest fully between games and check with a doctor first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or joint issues. It is an untested concept and easy to overdo, so keep easy days between sessions.
modalities.tweet: Experimental format: Tiny Field Blitz. Three against three on a field a quarter of the normal size, 4-minute games, constant sprinting and nowhere to hide. For fit people short on time who want their whole brain and body in every second. ⚡

modalities.name: Shared Grind Training
modalities.tagline: Hard team conditioning where effort, not chat, builds the bond.
modalities.whatItIs: Shared Grind Training is team conditioning: a squad works through structured, demanding drills together, with little talking and a strong shared rhythm. It pushes team sport away from socializing, which builds connection through conversation, toward connection through common effort. Sessions are more structured and more physical than a normal practice.
modalities.coreIdea: Going through something hard side by side, at the same moment, can bond people in a way that conversation alone does not.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week a team meets for 60 minutes and follows a posted plan: a warm-up, then sprint ladders, shuttle runs and body-weight circuits done in unison, with nobody resting until the whole group has finished the set. Talk is limited to counting and encouragement. The last five minutes are a slow walk and stretch in a circle.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who bond better by doing than by talking, and teams that want to feel more united.
modalities.cautions: Hard, repeated conditioning raises the risk of overexertion, strains and, rarely, dangerous muscle breakdown, so increase volume gradually, never push through sharp pain, drink water and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. Pressure to keep up can be risky, so anyone can switch to an easier version at any time; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: An idea for teams: Shared Grind Training. Hard, structured conditioning done in unison, with nobody resting until the whole group finishes the set. Little talk, lots of shared effort. For people who bond by doing hard things side by side.

modalities.name: Indoor Court League
modalities.tagline: Fast team games on a marked indoor court under lights.
modalities.whatItIs: Indoor Court League takes team sport indoors to a marked court with clear lines, timed halves and a scoreboard, played whatever the weather. It pushes team sport away from open, unstructured walks in nature, toward a controlled, predictable and highly structured space. There is nothing to look at but the game.
modalities.coreIdea: A closed, predictable environment removes distractions and surprises, so all attention and energy go into the play.
modalities.whatYouDo: Teams of five meet weekly in a sports hall for two 20-minute halves with a timer and scoreboard, plus fixed substitutions every four minutes. Warm-ups follow the same routine every week, and the season runs on a published schedule with standings. Sessions last about 75 minutes, including a group stretch.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like predictable routines, dislike bad weather and uneven ground, or find open spaces distracting.
modalities.cautions: Hard indoor floors and fast turns raise the risk of ankle and knee injuries, so wear proper indoor shoes, warm up, play no-contact and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea and is no substitute for care you may need for anxiety or low mood.
modalities.tweet: Prototype league: Indoor Court League. Fast five-a-side team games on a marked court, timed halves, a scoreboard and the same warm-up every week, rain or shine. For people who play best when the world is predictable and nothing distracts from the game.

modalities.name: Huddle and Execute
modalities.tagline: Team games with quick tactical huddles, then full-speed play.
modalities.whatItIs: Huddle and Execute is a team game with built-in tactical huddles: every few points, each team gets 60 seconds to plan, then plays the plan at full speed. It moves team sport away from slow, quiet sensory mindfulness, toward active thinking, planning and fast execution together. The mind is as involved as the legs.
modalities.coreIdea: Alternating short bursts of joint planning with full-speed action trains a team to think together fast and then commit.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 90-minute session, two teams of seven play, and after every third point the game pauses for a 60-second huddle in which any player can propose a tactic. The team picks one and runs it, then checks in the next huddle whether it worked. A whiteboard beside the field helps teams sketch ideas.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy strategy and teamwork, and anyone who wants practice making quick group decisions.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings injury risk, so warm up, play no-contact, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and pressure to deliver the plan can feel stressful, so keep the tone friendly.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Huddle and Execute. A team game that pauses every three points for a 60-second huddle. Anyone can pitch a tactic, the team picks one, then everyone runs it at full speed. For strategy lovers who want to think together fast, then commit.

modalities.name: Rotating Captain Season
modalities.tagline: Every player takes a turn leading the team.
modalities.whatItIs: Rotating Captain Season is a way of running a recreational team in which leadership passes to a new player every session. That player leads the warm-up, picks the drills, calls the lines and runs the end-of-game circle. It pushes team sport away from expert-led practices such as music therapy, toward shared, self-led structure in which everyone both leads and follows.
modalities.coreIdea: Taking turns leading peers, in a setting with clear roles, lets everyone practice speaking up, making calls and being followed.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the start of a season the team draws up a rota so that each player captains at least once. The captain arrives with a simple plan on a card (warm-up, two drills and the lines for the game) and the team follows it without debate. After each session the captain gets two pieces of praise and one suggestion from teammates.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rarely get to lead or want confidence speaking up in groups, and teams that lean too much on one person.
modalities.cautions: New captains may plan sessions that are too hard, so keep a shared list of safe warm-ups and drills, stop after any blow to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Leading can feel stressful for some, so swaps should be allowed; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: What if every player got to be captain for a day? Rotating Captain Season is an untested idea: each session a different teammate plans the warm-up, picks the drills and calls the lines. For people who rarely lead and want a friendly place to practice.

modalities.name: Unrun Ground
modalities.tagline: Every run covers ground you have never run before.
modalities.whatItIs: Unrun Ground is a self-led running practice with one rule: each run goes somewhere you have not run before, chosen at the door. It pushes endurance running away from imagery and history-focused therapy such as Ideal Parent Figure work, toward plain present-moment contact with real terrain, harder effort and no plan or guide at all. The newness of the route keeps attention outward.
modalities.coreIdea: New ground makes you look, choose and respond in real time, so the run stays in the present instead of on autopilot or inside your head.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you head out for 30 to 50 minutes in a direction you have not run before, picking turns as you go at a hard but steady effort. You carry a phone for safety and maps, checking it at junctions rather than following a set route. Over time you build a personal map of new streets, paths and trails.
modalities.whoItsFor: People bored by the same routes, runners who go through the motions on autopilot, and anyone who wants running to feel like exploring.
modalities.cautions: Unknown routes bring traffic, uneven ground and the risk of getting lost, so share your plan, carry a phone, run in daylight, avoid unsafe areas, build effort gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for professional care.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Unrun Ground. Every run goes somewhere you have never run before, decided at the door. No set route, no plan, just new streets and trails and eyes on what is in front of you. For runners stuck on autopilot who want it to feel like exploring. 🧭

modalities.name: Gradient Chaser
modalities.tagline: Seek out the hilliest route and let the climbs set the effort.
modalities.whatItIs: Gradient Chaser is a running practice built around hills: you plan routes with as much climbing as you can find and push steadily up every one. It moves endurance away from inward parts work such as Internal Family Systems, toward outward, wholehearted effort that the terrain itself demands. There are few rules, because the gradient does the planning.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting the hill set the effort gives you one clear challenge at a time outside yourself, and committing to it fully leaves little room for inner debate.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you run a 40 to 60 minute route chosen for its climbs, pushing hard but steadily on each uphill and jogging easily on the way down. You keep your eyes on the next crest and notice the moment of reaching the top. Over the weeks you seek out longer or steeper hills, building up gradually.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who like a challenge they can see, and anyone whose head gets busy on flat, steady runs.
modalities.cautions: Hard climbs put extra load on the heart, calves and Achilles tendons, and descents strain the knees, so build up slowly, walk the steepest parts when needed and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea and does not replace any care you already have.
modalities.tweet: Idea for runners: Gradient Chaser. Plan the hilliest route you can find and let every climb set the effort. One clear challenge at a time, eyes on the next crest. For people whose minds get busy on flat runs and who like a challenge they can see.

modalities.name: Data-Free Effort
modalities.tagline: Hard runs with no watch, app, log or plan.
modalities.whatItIs: Data-Free Effort is running stripped of every measurement: no watch, no app, no log, no target and no planned route. It pushes endurance as far as possible from structured, goal-tracking therapy such as CBT, toward an open practice in which effort is judged only by the body. Runs can still be hard, but nothing is recorded.
modalities.coreIdea: Without numbers to check or goals to meet, a run stops being a test and becomes an experience, judged only by how it feels.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you leave every device at home, apart from a phone kept in a pocket for safety if you want one. You run as long and as hard as feels right, speeding up and easing off by feel, and turn back when you choose. Afterward you record nothing at all.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have become anxious about pace, data or streaks, and anyone who feels their running has turned into homework.
modalities.cautions: Without tracking it is easy to overdo distance or effort, so keep most runs moderate, take rest days, carry ID, tell someone your rough route and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for help if exercise has become compulsive.
modalities.tweet: An idea for data-tired runners: Data-Free Effort. No watch, no app, no log, no plan. Run as hard and as long as feels right, then record nothing. For anyone whose running has become a spreadsheet and who wants it to feel like their own again.

modalities.name: State Shift Running
modalities.tagline: Run on purpose to change how you feel, then notice.
modalities.whatItIs: State Shift Running uses a run as a deliberate attempt to change your state rather than sit with it: you head out when you feel flat, tense or foggy and keep going until something shifts. It moves endurance away from acceptance-based therapy such as ACT, which teaches making room for feelings, toward actively moving them through effort. A one-word check before and after keeps it honest.
modalities.coreIdea: A run can be an action you take on purpose to move your state, and noting the before and after shows you what actually happens.
modalities.whatYouDo: When you notice you feel flat or wound up, you write one word for your state, then run hard but steadily for 20 to 45 minutes without headphones. When you notice a shift, or when time is up, you ease off and write a second word. After a month you look back at the pairs of words to see what tends to change.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want an active, practical response to low energy or tension, and who like to see for themselves what works.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea: if low mood or anxiety persists, talk to a doctor or therapist rather than relying on running alone.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: State Shift Running. Write one word for how you feel, run hard until something shifts, then write another word. After a month you have your own record of what a run does for you. For people who want to act on a bad day, not wait it out.

modalities.name: Same Loop Again
modalities.tagline: One short loop, run again and again, until only rhythm remains.
modalities.whatItIs: Same Loop Again is a deliberately monotonous running practice: you run one short loop over and over for the whole session. It pushes endurance away from meaning-seeking, emotionally deep therapy such as Coherence Therapy, toward plain repetition of effort with nothing new to see or figure out. Without scenery or decisions, attention settles on rhythm, breath and effort.
modalities.coreIdea: When the route offers nothing new, there is nothing left to interpret, and the run becomes pure repetition and rhythm.
modalities.whatYouDo: You pick a safe loop of 400 meters to 1 kilometer, such as a track or a park path, and run it again and again for 30 to 60 minutes at a hard, steady effort. You do not count laps or check splits, and when your mind drifts to the boredom you return to the sound of your breath and footsteps. Once a week is enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who overanalyze, who want a simple practice with no decisions, or who are curious what happens when boredom is allowed.
modalities.cautions: Running the same loop, especially on a track, loads the same tissues over and over, so change direction every few laps, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea and the boredom is part of it, but stop if it feels distressing rather than dull.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what happens if you run the same short loop for 45 minutes? Same Loop Again strips away scenery, decisions and novelty until only rhythm, breath and effort are left. A new practice for overthinkers who want something simple.

modalities.name: One Cue Running
modalities.tagline: Every run, one deliberate form cue, refined minute by minute.
modalities.whatItIs: One Cue Running is a practice of deliberate control over how you run: each session focuses on a single form cue, such as tall posture or quick, light steps. It moves endurance away from involuntary, let-it-happen body work such as TRE, where the body shakes by itself, toward conscious shaping of movement. Attention moves between the body and the cue rather than out to the scenery.
modalities.coreIdea: Choosing how your body moves, one cue at a time, turns running into a practice of skillful, voluntary control.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before each 30 to 45 minute run you pick one cue, such as relaxed shoulders, quiet feet or arms swinging straight forward and back. Every minute or so you return to it and make a small adjustment, and in the last ten minutes you notice whether it now happens by itself. You choose a new cue each week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who like technique and craft, and anyone who wants a sense of skill and control in their body.
modalities.cautions: Big, sudden changes to running form can cause new aches or injuries, so keep changes small, keep effort moderate at first and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and form work does not replace advice from a physiotherapist for pain or injury.
modalities.tweet: New idea: One Cue Running. Each run, pick one form cue (tall posture, quiet feet, relaxed hands) and return to it every minute until it starts to happen by itself. For runners who love craft and want to feel more skillful and in control of their body.

modalities.name: Strong Finish Practice
modalities.tagline: Steady runs where the last third always gets faster.
modalities.whatItIs: Strong Finish Practice is a simple running rule: you start every run easily and make the final third faster, finishing stronger than you started. It moves endurance away from slow, receptive inner work such as Focusing, which waits for a shift to come, toward deliberately building momentum. The structure is light: one rule, applied every time.
modalities.coreIdea: Finishing stronger than you started, again and again, gives a repeated, bodily experience of building momentum rather than fading.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 50 minutes, the first two thirds at an easy, conversational pace and the last third building steadily toward a hard effort. You end with a few minutes of walking. Over the weeks the finishing section can get a little longer or faster.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to start things too fast and then fade, and runners who want the feeling of finishing well.
modalities.cautions: Hard finishes add strain on the heart and muscles, so build up over weeks, keep at least one rest day between sessions and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Strong Finish Practice. Start every run easy and make the last third faster, every single time. A simple rule for people who tend to start things hot and fade, and who want to practice finishing stronger than they began.

modalities.name: Your Own Coach
modalities.tagline: A ten-week block where you plan, log and adjust yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Your Own Coach is a self-coaching practice for runners: for ten weeks you write your own plan, log each run and review it every week, adjusting as you go. It pushes endurance away from presence-based coaching such as Aletheia, which relies on a coach and avoids self-improvement, toward deliberate, self-led improvement. The skill being built is coaching yourself.
modalities.coreIdea: Planning, reviewing and adjusting your own training builds the habit of setting a direction and steering by what actually happens.
modalities.whatYouDo: In week one you choose a goal, such as running 10 kilometers without stopping, and write a simple ten-week plan of three runs a week. After each run you log the time, your effort out of ten and one note, and every Sunday you review the week and change the next week's plan if needed. In week ten you write a short letter to yourself about what you learned.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like planning and ownership, and runners who want to stop depending on apps or coaches.
modalities.cautions: Self-written plans often build up too fast, so add no more than about 10 percent a week, include rest days and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and tracking can turn compulsive for some people, so take a break if the log starts to feel like pressure.
modalities.tweet: Proposed practice: Your Own Coach. Ten weeks where you write the plan, log every run and review it each Sunday. The real goal is learning to steer by what actually happens. For people tired of following apps who want to own their training.

modalities.name: Exact Pace Practice
modalities.tagline: Hold one precise pace, correcting at every marker.
modalities.whatItIs: Exact Pace Practice is running as precise control: you pick a pace and hold it within a few seconds at every marker, correcting all the way. It pushes endurance as far as it goes from Do Nothing meditation, in which nothing is steered, toward continuous, deliberate self-regulation. Effort is high and attention never leaves the task.
modalities.coreIdea: Holding an exact pace means noticing tiny drifts and correcting them, a moment-by-moment practice of steering yourself.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a track or a measured path you run for 20 to 40 minutes at a chosen target pace, checking your time at each marker, such as every 400 meters on a track, and nudging faster or slower. You aim to finish with every split within five seconds of the target. Afterward you note which parts drifted and why.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy precision and control, and runners who want to learn pacing.
modalities.cautions: Hard, sustained efforts strain the heart and muscles, so choose a pace that is challenging but sustainable, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and if the need for control starts to feel rigid or anxious, ease off.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Exact Pace Practice. Pick a pace, hold it within five seconds at every marker, notice each drift and correct it. Running as a moment-by-moment exercise in steering yourself. For precision lovers and anyone learning to pace a run.

modalities.name: Panorama Pace
modalities.tagline: Running hard with a soft, wide gaze on everything around.
modalities.whatItIs: Panorama Pace is a running practice of wide, outward attention: instead of narrowing your focus or turning inward, you keep a soft gaze that takes in your whole field of view. It moves endurance away from metta and jhana meditation, which settle deeply on one warm inner feeling, toward open, panoramic contact with the world while working hard. Structure is minimal.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping attention wide and outward during hard effort keeps you in contact with your surroundings instead of shrinking into the discomfort.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a familiar, safe route you run for 30 to 45 minutes at a hard, steady effort while softening your gaze, so that you notice movement and color at the edges of your vision. Whenever attention narrows onto the effort or a thought, you widen it again to the whole scene. Open parks, beaches and riverside paths work best.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose attention narrows under stress, and runners who want to feel more connected to where they are.
modalities.cautions: A wide gaze must never replace watching your footing and traffic, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for professional care.
modalities.tweet: What if you ran with your attention as wide as the sky? Panorama Pace is a new practice: hard, steady running with a soft gaze that takes in the whole scene, widening again whenever your focus shrinks. For anyone whose world gets small when things get hard.

modalities.name: Self-Talk Surges
modalities.tagline: Chosen words, said under your breath, on every hard stretch.
modalities.whatItIs: Self-Talk Surges is a running practice in which you actively talk yourself through effort, using a few phrases chosen in advance. It moves endurance away from vipassana, which trains watching experience without reacting, toward engaging with it and pushing back. The runs are hard and loosely structured, and the phrases come out whenever the going gets tough.
modalities.coreIdea: Choosing your own words for hard moments, and saying them as you go, is practice in meeting difficulty with an active, encouraging voice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a run you write down three short phrases, such as 'strong and steady' or 'one more hill', and learn them by heart. During a 30 to 45 minute run with hard stretches, you say them under your breath each time the effort rises, and afterward you note which phrase helped most. You refresh the phrases each month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose inner critic gets loud during effort, and anyone who wants practice speaking to themselves more kindly and firmly.
modalities.cautions: Talking yourself past your limits can lead to overexertion, so keep the phrases encouraging rather than punishing, respect pain and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea and no replacement for therapy if self-criticism is severe.
modalities.tweet: Fresh concept: Self-Talk Surges. Write three short phrases before you run, then say them under your breath every time it gets hard. For anyone whose inner voice turns harsh mid-effort and who wants practice talking to themselves like a good coach.

modalities.name: All-Day Shuffle
modalities.tagline: A jog so easy you could keep going for hours.
modalities.whatItIs: All-Day Shuffle is endurance at its gentlest: a very easy, unstructured jog-walk, slow enough that you feel you could keep going all day. It moves running away from high-intensity interval training, toward lower effort, calmer activation and no structure at all. Walking breaks are welcome and pace does not matter.
modalities.coreIdea: Time on your feet at an effortless pace lets you move for a long time without strain, and shows that movement does not have to be hard to count.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you go out for 45 to 90 minutes and shuffle at a pace where you could chat or hum, walking whenever you like. There are no intervals, targets or route plans. You stop while it still feels easy.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find running too hard or intense workouts unpleasant, people returning to exercise, and anyone who wants a calm way to move for longer.
modalities.cautions: Even slow, long outings can cause blisters, aches or overuse injuries if you build up too fast, so increase time gradually, drink water and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Hate hard workouts? Here's a new concept: All-Day Shuffle. A jog so easy you could keep it up for hours, walking breaks welcome, no intervals and no targets. Movement that doesn't have to hurt to count.

modalities.name: Far From Anyone
modalities.tagline: Long solo runs where being alone is the whole point.
modalities.whatItIs: Far From Anyone is a running practice built around solitude: long, steady runs alone, ideally somewhere quiet, with no company, no calls and no group. It pushes endurance away from team sport, toward full aloneness and inward attention. Thoughts are allowed to come and go.
modalities.coreIdea: Regular, chosen solitude in motion gives space for your own thoughts and rhythm, apart from anyone else's needs or opinions.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you run for 45 to 90 minutes at a steady, comfortable effort on a quiet route, leaving headphones behind and setting your phone to emergency calls only. You let thoughts arise and pass without trying to solve them. Afterward some people write a few lines about what came to mind.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are surrounded by others all day, such as carers, parents and people in customer-facing jobs, and anyone who wants regular time alone.
modalities.cautions: Running alone in quiet places carries extra safety risks, so tell someone your route and return time, carry a phone and ID, avoid isolated places after dark, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and if solitude starts to feel like withdrawal, reach out to people and talk to someone.
modalities.tweet: Sketch of a new practice: Far From Anyone. A long weekly run, alone, somewhere quiet, with no headphones, no group and no calls. For people who are needed by others all day and want one block of time where their thoughts and rhythm belong only to them.

modalities.name: Breath Sets the Pace
modalities.tagline: Let your breathing, not a plan, decide how fast you run.
modalities.whatItIs: Breath Sets the Pace is a loose running practice in which your breathing is the only guide to speed: ease off when it turns ragged, lift when it feels easy. It moves endurance away from structured, load-counting strength training, toward an open, allowing approach with no sets, numbers or targets. Attention rests partly on the breath and partly on the route.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting the breath decide the pace turns each run into a conversation with your body instead of a plan to complete.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 25 to 45 minutes without a watch or plan, tuning in to your breathing every minute or so. If breathing turns ragged you slow down or walk, and if it feels smooth and easy you pick up a little. The run ends when you have had enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who push too hard, feel bossed around by training plans, or want running to feel more natural.
modalities.cautions: Breathing is a rough guide and can lag behind effort, so start gently, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or other health problems, including asthma. It is an untested idea and does not replace medical advice.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Breath Sets the Pace. No watch, no plan. Ease off when your breathing turns ragged, lift when it feels easy, stop when you've had enough. For runners who feel bossed around by training plans and want a run that listens to their body.

modalities.name: Carry One Question
modalities.tagline: Take one question on a hard solo run, and see what comes.
modalities.whatItIs: Carry One Question is a solo running practice that pairs hard effort with a single question you take along, such as a decision or a puzzle. It moves endurance away from animal-assisted therapy, with its calm companionship and outward attention, toward solitary, effortful thinking time. The run is part physical challenge, part private thinking space.
modalities.coreIdea: A hard run with one question in mind gives the mind room to turn it over while the body is busy, and some people find it looks different afterward.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before you go, you write one question on a card, such as 'what do I want from this job?', and leave it at home. You run for 30 to 50 minutes alone at a hard, steady pace, coming back to the question whenever your mind wanders. When you get home, you spend five minutes writing down whatever came up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think better on the move, and anyone stuck on a decision who wants a different way to approach it.
modalities.cautions: Being lost in thought on a hard run makes you less alert to traffic and terrain, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and big personal decisions may still need talking through with someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Carry One Question. Write one question on a card, leave it at home, then go for a hard solo run and let your mind turn it over. Write down what came up when you get back. For people who think best when their legs are busy.

modalities.name: Run to Somewhere
modalities.tagline: Runs that always go from one place to another, never loops.
modalities.whatItIs: Run to Somewhere is endurance running as a journey: every run goes from one place to another, such as from home to work, to a friend's house or to a train station, never in a loop. It moves running away from slow, calm, set-form practices such as qigong, done in one spot, toward energetic, unplanned travel across ground. The destination gives the run its purpose.
modalities.coreIdea: Running to a real destination turns exercise into getting somewhere, which gives each run a story with a beginning and an end.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you replace a journey with a run of 20 to 60 minutes, carrying a light backpack with essentials and taking transport back if needed. You choose the route on the day, and arriving is the finish line. Some people run to meet friends for breakfast or to end at a swimming pool.
modalities.whoItsFor: Busy people who struggle to find time, and anyone who finds loops pointless and loves the feeling of arriving.
modalities.cautions: Running with a pack and through traffic adds strain and risk, so keep the pack light, use safe routes, wear bright clothing, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Run to Somewhere. No loops, ever. Every run takes you to a real place (work, a friend, a cafe, the station) and arriving is the finish line. For people who find running in circles pointless and love the feeling of getting somewhere.

modalities.name: Lone Clock Trial
modalities.tagline: A monthly solo test against your own clock.
modalities.whatItIs: Lone Clock Trial is a monthly solo time trial: you run the same measured course alone at your best sustainable effort and compare only with your own earlier times. It moves endurance away from socializing, toward solitude, independence and clear structure, with no pack to pull you along or hide in. Between trials you train however you like.
modalities.coreIdea: Testing yourself alone, on the same course, with nobody watching, builds a private and honest relationship with your own effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a safe, flat course of 3 to 5 kilometers and, once a month after a good warm-up, run it as fast as you can sustain, timing yourself. You write the time and one sentence about how it felt in a notebook kept only for this. Over a year the notebook becomes a record of your own effort, good months and bad.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who dislike group races or comparison, and anyone who wants a private challenge that comes round every month.
modalities.cautions: Hard solo efforts strain the heart and muscles and nobody is there if something goes wrong, so tell someone when and where you are running, carry a phone, build fitness first and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and if the results start to drive your self-worth, take a break.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: Lone Clock Trial. Once a month, run the same course alone as hard as you can sustain, time it and write one sentence in a notebook. No pack, no audience, no comparisons. For people who want an honest, private challenge.

modalities.name: Blank Wall Treadmill
modalities.tagline: Treadmill runs facing a plain wall, with nothing to watch.
modalities.whatItIs: Blank Wall Treadmill is indoor endurance running with all scenery removed: you run on a treadmill facing a plain wall, with no screen, music or view. It pushes endurance away from nature walks, with their open, changing scenery, toward a controlled, structured space in which the effort is the whole experience. Attention turns inward, to breath, effort and thought.
modalities.coreIdea: With nothing outside to look at, the effort itself becomes the whole experience, and you practice staying with it on purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you run for 20 to 40 minutes on a treadmill turned to face a wall, following a simple set plan such as five easy minutes, a hard steady middle and five easy minutes. You cover the console so only the timer shows. Whenever you want to escape, you notice the urge and return to your breath.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to practice staying with discomfort without distraction, and anyone who can only exercise indoors.
modalities.cautions: Treadmills carry a fall risk, so use the safety clip, keep the handrails within reach, build effort gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and the monotony can feel unpleasant, so keep sessions short at first.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if you ran on a treadmill facing a blank wall, with no screen, music or view? Blank Wall Treadmill makes the effort itself the whole experience. For people who want to practice staying with something hard, without escape.

modalities.name: Story Miles
modalities.tagline: Long, hard runs where your mind travels in a story.
modalities.whatItIs: Story Miles pairs long, hard runs with a gripping audiobook or story podcast, so your attention lives in the story while your body works. It moves endurance away from sensory mindfulness, which anchors attention in raw sensation, toward imagination and narrative. The effort is high, but the mind is somewhere else entirely.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting a story carry the mind may make long, hard effort feel shorter, and gives each run something to look forward to.
modalities.whatYouDo: You save a story you love for running only and listen to one chapter per run of 40 to 70 minutes at a steady, hard effort. You use open-ear headphones or a single earbud so you can still hear traffic. If you skip a run, the story waits too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find long runs boring, and anyone who wants a reason to look forward to going out.
modalities.cautions: Audio reduces awareness of traffic and other people, so keep the volume low, use open-ear headphones on quiet, safe routes, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and low volume also protects your hearing.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Story Miles 🎧 Save a gripping audiobook for runs only, one chapter per outing, so the story pulls you out of the door and through the hard miles. For people who find long runs boring and want a reason to look forward to them.

modalities.name: Footfall Soundtrack
modalities.tagline: No headphones: your breath and footsteps are the music.
modalities.whatItIs: Footfall Soundtrack is running without any music or audio, using the sound of your own breath and footsteps as the rhythm. It moves endurance away from music-based practices, toward self-led, solitary running in which the only beat comes from your body. The effort is hard and steady.
modalities.coreIdea: Listening to your own rhythm, instead of following a soundtrack, makes running a direct conversation with your body's pace.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 50 minutes without headphones at a hard, steady effort, tuning your attention to the pattern of your footsteps and breathing, such as three steps in and three steps out. When the rhythm changes on hills or turns, you notice it change. Some people end with a minute of standing still, listening to their heartbeat settle.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who always need music to get going, and anyone who wants a simpler, quieter way to run.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so warm up, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Footfall Soundtrack. Leave the headphones at home and let your breath and footsteps be the beat. Three steps in, three steps out, changing on every hill. For runners who never go without music and want to hear their own rhythm for once.

modalities.name: Stones and Sandbags
modalities.tagline: A strict, self-run plan for lifting real, awkward objects.
modalities.whatItIs: Stones and Sandbags is strength training with real-world objects instead of barbells: sandbags, stones, water containers and a loaded backpack, lifted on a strict, self-written progression. It pushes strength training away from imagined, history-focused therapy such as Ideal Parent Figure work, toward plain contact with the weight of real things. There is no imagery and no story, only an object you can see, grip and feel.
modalities.coreIdea: Lifting real, awkward objects keeps attention entirely on what is in your hands right now, and progress is as tangible as the load.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, in a yard or a park, you lift, carry and load a set of objects of known weight following a written plan, for example sandbag lifts to the shoulder, carries and squats, 3 to 5 sets each. Each week you add a little weight, such as a liter of water or a kilogram of sand, and write it down. Sessions take 40 to 50 minutes and you run them yourself.
modalities.whoItsFor: People bored by gyms, those who want strength that shows up in daily life, and anyone who likes simple, tangible progress.
modalities.cautions: Awkward objects shift and are harder to lift safely than bars, so learn safe lifting first, start light, keep your back neutral and drop the object if you need to; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for professional care.
modalities.tweet: Invented practice: Stones and Sandbags. A strict, self-run strength plan with real objects (sandbags, water jugs, stones) and a little more weight each week. No imagery, no story, just something heavy and real in your hands. For people who find gyms dull.

modalities.name: Single Lift Season
modalities.tagline: Eight weeks devoted to mastering just one lift.
modalities.whatItIs: Single Lift Season is a strength block devoted to one movement, such as the squat or the deadlift, practiced every session for eight weeks. It pushes strength training away from parts work such as Internal Family Systems, which explores many inner voices, toward undivided focus on one task, with maximal structure and a clear aim of change. Everything else in training is kept to a minimum.
modalities.coreIdea: Pouring all your effort into one movement, again and again, gives a rare experience of wholehearted, undivided focus and visible mastery.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose one lift and practice it three times a week from a written plan: a long warm-up, technique sets, then 3 to 5 working sets, adding a little weight only when every rep is clean. You film one set a week to check your form. After eight weeks you test a comfortable five-rep set and compare it with week one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer depth to variety, and anyone who wants to know what mastering one thing feels like.
modalities.cautions: Repeating one movement often can overload the same joints, so keep loads moderate, warm up thoroughly, learn the technique from a qualified coach first and stop with sharp pain; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure or heart problems should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Single Lift Season. Pick one lift, practice it three times a week for eight weeks, film your form and add weight only when every rep is clean. For people who'd rather go deep on one thing than dabble, and want to feel real mastery.

modalities.name: Feel First Lifting
modalities.tagline: The body's feedback, not the plan, sets today's weight.
modalities.whatItIs: Feel First Lifting is strength training in which the day's loads are chosen by how your warm-up sets feel, rather than by a written plan. It moves strength training a little away from structured, thought-checking therapy such as CBT, toward listening to the body and self-led judgment. The exercises stay the same while the numbers flex.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting bodily feedback set the load builds trust in your own signals and fits each session to the day you are actually having.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each session you warm up on your main lifts with gradually heavier sets and rate how each one feels on a scale of 1 to 10. You then pick a working weight that feels like a 7 or 8 out of 10, with two or three reps left in reserve, and do your sets. On tired days you go lighter and on good days heavier, without guilt either way.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel bossed around by programs, those whose energy varies a lot, and lifters who want to trust their own judgment.
modalities.cautions: Judging effort takes practice and beginners often misjudge it, so learn technique first, keep a couple of reps in reserve and never lift to failure alone; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Feel First Lifting. Same exercises every session, but the weight is set by how your warm-up feels today, not by the plan. Lighter on tired days, heavier on good ones, no guilt. For lifters who want to trust their own body.

modalities.name: Fixed Five Routine
modalities.tagline: The same five lifts, same order, every session, for months.
modalities.whatItIs: Fixed Five Routine is strength training as a fixed ritual: the same five lifts in the same order every session, with only the weight changing. It pushes strength training away from flexibility-focused therapy such as ACT, which values adapting to each moment, toward complete predictability, maximal structure and steady gains in strength. There are no decisions to make.
modalities.coreIdea: An unchanging routine removes choice and doubt, so you can simply show up and do it, and progress shows clearly against a background that never changes.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you do the same five movements, such as a squat, a press, a row, a hip hinge and a carry, for 3 sets of 5 to 8 reps, always in the same order. When all sets feel solid, you add the smallest possible weight next time. Each session takes about 45 minutes and goes on the same log sheet.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find decisions draining, those who like ritual and predictability, and beginners who want one simple plan.
modalities.cautions: Doing the same lifts for months can lead to overuse aches, so warm up, add weight in small steps, take a lighter week every month or two and learn technique from a qualified coach first; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure or heart problems should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: Fixed Five Routine. The same five lifts, in the same order, every session, for months, and only the weight changes. No choices, no doubts, just show up. For people who find decisions exhausting and want one simple ritual to stick to.

modalities.name: The Iron Ledger
modalities.tagline: Every set written down, and the record tells the story.
modalities.whatItIs: The Iron Ledger is a self-run strength practice centered on a paper ledger: every set, rep and weight is written down, and two simple rules decide when to progress. It moves strength training away from therapy that looks for hidden emotional meaning, such as Coherence Therapy, toward a plain, factual record with nothing to interpret. The numbers speak, and you follow them.
modalities.coreIdea: A plain written record shows effort and progress as facts, which can be steadying when your own judgment of yourself is unreliable.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before each session you copy last time's numbers onto a new line, then lift, aiming to beat one number by one rep or a small amount of weight. You follow two rules: add weight when you reach the top of the rep range on every set, and repeat the weight when you do not. Once a month you read back through the ledger.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who discount their own progress, those who prefer facts to feelings, and lifters who want a simple, honest record.
modalities.cautions: Chasing a better number every time can push you into poor form or overload, so allow repeat days, take lighter weeks and stop with pain; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure or heart problems should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and if the ledger starts to feel like a judge, put it away for a while.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: The Iron Ledger. Write down every set, rep and weight in a paper notebook and let two simple rules decide when to add weight. No interpreting, just facts. For people who never believe their own progress and want proof on paper.

modalities.name: Slow Control Reps
modalities.tagline: Very slow repetitions, every inch of movement chosen.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Control Reps is strength training done very slowly, with full, deliberate control of every part of each repetition. It moves strength training away from involuntary, let-the-body-shake practices such as TRE, toward complete voluntary control. Attention turns partly inward, to the muscles doing the work.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving a weight slowly and precisely, by choice, is a practice of voluntary control over your body under load.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you do six exercises with moderate loads, lowering each weight for four seconds, pausing for one and lifting for two, for 2 or 3 sets of 6 to 8 reps. A metronome app or quiet counting keeps the tempo. You keep breathing steadily and end each set before your form breaks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a calmer, more controlled way to get stronger, and anyone who feels their body sometimes runs away with them.
modalities.cautions: Slow reps feel hard and tempt people to hold their breath, which raises blood pressure, so keep breathing and use moderate weights; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea and does not replace physiotherapy for injuries.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Slow Control Reps. Four seconds down, one second pause, two seconds up, with every rep chosen on purpose. Strength training as a practice in controlling your own body. For people who want to feel steady and in charge under load.

modalities.name: Fast Bar Practice
modalities.tagline: Moderate weights, moved as fast as good form allows.
modalities.whatItIs: Fast Bar Practice is strength training built on explosive intent: moderate loads moved as fast as possible with good form, in short, crisp sets. It pushes strength training away from slow, receptive practices such as Focusing, which wait for a felt shift, toward decisive, immediate action. Each rep is a small, clear decision to go.
modalities.coreIdea: Approaching every rep as a decisive burst of intent is meant to build the habit of committing fully and fast.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you do 4 to 6 exercises, such as squats, push-ups and medicine-ball throws, with weights you could lift about ten times, but you do only 3 reps per set, each as fast as you can. You rest a full minute or two between sets so every rep stays crisp. A coach or a video checks your form every few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hesitate, procrastinate or overthink, and athletes who want more power.
modalities.cautions: Fast lifts put more stress on joints and tendons, so learn them from a qualified coach, use moderate loads, warm up well and stop if your form slips; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
